Acceptance algorithm traditionally demands complete and ranked preference lists from each party. However, studies have shown that stable matchings are achieved even with shorter, albeit incomplete, preference lists, thus sparking curiosity as to why and how agents should optimize these lists for the best possible matches. To address this question, the present work defines the optimization problem as a sequential game with the present-day assignments as its starting point. By applying tools from game theory, the research demonstrates that this optimization problem is most effectively solved by adopting a strategy called Randomized Restarting Deep Q-learning (RR-DQN), a variation of a well-known AI algorithm, and shows it surpasses the performance of a competing algorithm, the Renting Mechanism. Furthermore, the research provides theoretical and empirical evidence that the proposed RR-DQN strategy is highly likely to converge towards optimal matching configurations, thus outperforming a previously established strategy known as Superrandom, which had been shown to achieve suboptimal results. These findings not only validate the potential effectiveness of AI-based approaches in optimizing preference lists for a specific application like Deferred Acceptance but also underscore the value of game theory as a means to explain and interpret the outcomes of such algorithms. Lastly, the research highlights the practical value of a new strategy, Variational Deep Q-learning (V-DQN), as a competing approach that can rival RR-DQN. Both studies described in this report, involving the analysis of both complete and incomplete preference lists, were performed using the Python language with the aid of standard libraries and the gymlib, torchlib, and transformers-lib tools. The present work was completed as part of a research project at the Technion - Israel Institute of Technology, where the contributing party received support from the support center for numerical calculations and the cluster 'PaceR'. Similar studies were previously published by the same supporting organization, including S. Meisner's work on the application of Deep Q-learning in the field of kidney exchange, as well as P. Dietterich and his research on the application of evolutionary algorithms in the field of college admissions. Those studies, however, were conducted over a decade ago and yielded less robust outcomes than the ones presented here. The research reported here is innovative in at least three ways: first, it involves the application of a specific AI algorithm for the optimization of incomplete preference lists; second, it uses game theory to explain its outcomes; and third, it achieves near-optimal results with the aid of a Deep Q-learning algorithm, a first of its kind in the field of matching problems

Recent advances in Deep Learning have the potential to significantly enhance wildfire detection, especially with the integration of visible and infrared imaging, thereby offering superior performance and reduced error rates compared to current methods. Although DL-based image fusion methods have been widely studied, they have yet to be rigorously evaluated in the context of fire imagery, and to date, no comprehensive dataset has been made available that features visible-infrared fire image fusion. Owing to the growing interest in simplifying complex DL models, we have chosen three cutting-edge fusion techniques and subjected them to thorough evaluation for their effectiveness in wildfire image fusion. Our comparative study introduces a novel, extensive dataset for evaluating the fusion of visible-infrared wildfire images, and through rigorous experimentation, it demonstrates that all DL models are capable of surpassing traditional image fusion methods in terms of performance. Our code and dataset are publicly available for further research. Ultimately, this study aims to foster more extensive and meaningful research in wildfire image fusion using DL techniques. Our contributions to this field are summarized as follows. Firstly, we have compiled a first-ever dataset of 3400 pairs of visible-infrared wildfire images, enabling a more accurate assessment of fire detection and objectness through infrared visibility enhancement. Secondly, we have successfully applied DL models to this specific task for the very first time, and our results reveal their superiority over existing image fusion methods. Lastly, this research serves as a critical evaluation of several prominent DL models, thereby offering valuable insights for the selection of suitable models for this specific task and offering potential avenues for further research in the future. While current systems utilize social media data to diagnose and comprehend mental health, accurately predicting depression is challenging due to the inherent subjectivity of emotions. A unique characteristic arises due to 2nd-order exceptional points, where an otherwise trivial band structure becomes topologically complex at higher energy levels. Absence of traditional symmetry in the model allows the emergence of fractional boundary states in the system. Moreover, another key aspect of the bulk-boundary correspondence is uncovered, where an extra exceptional point in the bulk material is safeguarded by its connection to boundary states. When certain drive is applied to the ring, it develops a dynamic Floquet topological state, where protected states at the drive frequency exclusively occupy the edge of the ring. Interestingly, this dynamic state can transition into a non-topological state through multiple suppression mechanisms, where high-frequency drive destroys the edge states, while low-frequency drive leads to a mirror-image revival of these states across the ring. Furthermore, we discover a self-dual state within the Floquet band, where edge states mirror their topological counterparts in both real and reciprocal spaces. annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although the problem is largely solved for contemporary languages, historical corpora pose significant challenges, primarily due to limited native speaker interaction and a lack of training data. Compounding this issue, historical texts lack standardized sentence structures and orthographies, making automated POS tagging more complex and error-prone. To address these complexities, this paper proposes a multi-step POS tagging approach for medieval Icelandic, initially involving word normalization, lemmatization, and sentence structure standardization. Utilizing a dataset of annotated Íslendinga-Þáttir, the scheme achieves POS tagging accuracy rates of up to 42.7% for each intermediate step. When combined, the steps yield a final accuracy rate of 34.6%, presenting a viable method for the POS tagging of standardized, but orthographically varied historical texts. Furthermore, this paper provides the train and test data, as well as the tagging scheme, for reproducibility, (available at https://github.com/finnbelle/pos-isn). Moreover, proposals are presented to address the primary issues encountered during this research: developing new training data, creating new models, and integrating them into tools for natural language processing. These proposals aim to enhance the usability of POS tagging for a range of contemporary historical languages. Based on the experience of this research project, suggestions for overcoming related challenges are outlined below. 1. By incorporating inverse gate implementations, noise levels are diminished and the robustness of the quantum circuit improves. This strategy proves particularly effective in multiple error scenarios, particularly where the noise factor and the gate's inverse have an inverse relationship. We successfully integrated this noise-mitigation approach within a variational quantum eigensolver running on a superconducting quantum processor to find the ground-state energy of the hydrogen molecule, and observed substantial energy fluctuations reductions during the parameter learning process in the VQE algorithm. These analyses reveal that while certain noise models may exhibit different behavior in response to the inverse gate, it is predominantly the dominant coherent error effect that yields the greatest robustness benefit. This discovery confirms the efficacy of the hidden inverse method as a universal error-reduction technique and makes it a more attractive option for practical quantum computing applications. This research is the first to implement this method on a real quantum device and is capable of supporting various noise models, thereby providing a comprehensive understanding of its performance. In light of the results presented here, it is now feasible to employ the hidden inverse method as a superior alternative to lower two-qubit error rates or more intricate multi-qubit error correction approaches, especially in the near-term quantum computing era. Furthermore, it is proposed that future implementations of this method could be optimized to reduce its overhead complexity, using techniques like gate concatenation or the use of reversible todlup gates, though such optimizations are still to be tested in practice and remain the subject of future research. Clebsch canonization has been proposed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent canonical Hamiltonian systems through a momentum map connection. We outline both an algebraic and a geometric approach to this method, with the latter presented here for the first time. Moreover, we discovered an additional momentum map, resulting in a dual pair of momentum maps in certain instances. This research offers a straightforward, unified framework for several previously reported canonical forms, while also enabling the preservation of key properties (e.g., geometric structure, symplectic invariants) in non-linear systems. We provide illustrative examples of Lie-Poisson systems where the Clebsch canonization can be applied. These include relativistic harmonic oscillators, free particles on the surface of a sphere in 2D and 3D space, and various spin systems, which cover a vast scope of physics from macro to quantum scales. We intend to expand upon this research in future work, particularly by examining bi-Hamiltonian systems and the respective multi-momentum maps. The underlying structure of the work can also be easily generalized to other types of Lie-Poisson systems. The corresponding paper can be found at arXiv:2106.16014 [math.OA]. Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation variations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel approach using traditional M\"{o}bius geometric transformations to constrain and align image representations with respect to orientation. By projecting image features onto a hypersphere, we have created the Orientation Alignment Loss (OAL) to capture direction-based information and weight the loss by orientation consistency, providing a comprehensive representation that encompasses both local low-level features and high-level semantic information. Experiment results demonstrate that our proposed OAL is more efficient in capturing orientation and outperforms other state-of-the-art methods on various benchmark datasets, both in classification and transfer learning applications. This unique loss is universally applicable and can be seamlessly integrated with any deep learning model without undergoing significant redesign. Furthermore, we have employed OAL to enhance the interoperability of cross-domain models by adapting image features to a geometrically consistent format, enabling cross-oriented operations. Our innovative cable-driven framework eliminates the need for corrective actions after each movement, integrating elasticity into theplanning stage to ensure precise tracking. The proposed solution involves two parts: Firstly, we can predict a robot's real positioning based on its designed path and an inverse-elastic model, allowing us to create adjusted trajectories that account for elasticity. The adjusted trajectories are optimized to minimize positioning errors while ensuring that the robot's limbs do not cross each other; we use a layering approach to efficiently find the optimal solution with an existing algorithm. The second step is a process where adjusted trajectories are calculated in real-time through a machine learning model, enabling the execution of the final trajectory with the actual hardware. The results show that our new planning framework significantly improves the tracking performance, especially for complex tasks with tight error tolerances, showing up to 86% better performance. Additionally, we found that this planning framework can be applied to execution without significant time increases. We also showed that our real-time learning approach, using plain, existing elasticity models, is enough to improve the performance of the robot's tracking, reducing its errors by up to 3.5% on average. If a more accurate model is available, the improvement is even better, reducing the robot's errors by 6.3% on average. Finally, we demonstrated that this planning framework can be adapted to different robotic architectures by successfully testing it on both spherical and universal joint robots. The knowledge and approaches developed in this study could be easily applied to other robotic architectures, potentially through a straightforward transfer. The code for this research is publicly available at: https://github.com/DanielFelaczez/elastic-cmd-pybullet. Despite this, current deep learning-based methods rely heavily on a vast quantity of high-quality, labeled images which often contains errors. Consequently, developing robust training techniques that minimize the negative effects of noisy labels is of the utmost importance for achieving optimal model performance. To this end, a supervised method referred to as ProD is proposed to tackle the problem of training from noisy labeled data. By leveraging additional clean samples obtained through data augmentation, ProD is able to accurately identify and distinguish between true samples and the artificial noise in the labels. By iteratively utilizing this insight to re-label the training data, the model is able to avoid overfitting and overcome the issues associated with noisy labels. Experimental results show that ProD is highly effective at removing label noise and achieving superior performance on various medical image classification tasks. Furthermore, the code and knowledge needed to implement the method are freely accessible at https://github.com/LucasChen-Tsao/ProD. We hope that this method may be utilized in a wide range of medical image classification applications to achieve the optimal outcome. We look forward to further exploring the capabilities of the method and will provide updates on any new developments. With regards to future work, we plan on modifying the method to address the specific challenges associated with label shift noise, where the probability distribution of the labels varies across different classes, as this would involve significant modifications to the ProD method as currently implemented. Alternatively, we may consider developing a new, variant of the method specifically designed to address label shift noise. Additionally, we would like to further investigate the potential of applying data augmentation to clean images as an alternative to re-labeling, as this could potentially reduce the influence of noisy labels on the model. 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: detecting and isolating individual characters within a crowd when the image contains scene text that is not fully captured.
Given a fragmented scene text, participants needed to predict the missing components and generate a complete sentence.
The OOV challenge was held in conjunction with the 15th Chinese Conference on Pattern Recognition & Computer Vision (PRCU 2022), featuring three tasks and an evaluation process that utilized a dataset of 10,000 scene text images.
This report provides an overview of the dataset, evaluation criteria, and winning solutions for each task.
Moreover, we discuss the winning algorithms and the common challenges encountered by participants. 
Finally, we outline potential avenues for future research and thank the organizers and fellow competitors for their efforts.

However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity were increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline. Consequently, the decline in urban diversity is largely attributed to altered attitudes and perceptions, not necessarily related to risk aversion, which may persist beyond the pandemic era. Therefore, potential long-term consequences of enhanced isolation and reduced willingness to explore new places should be closely monitored. To mitigate these effects, restoring a diverse urban environment can be facilitated by restoring a balanced visitation pattern that effectively combines predictability (home and routine visits) with curiosity-driven exploration of new places. This might involve restoring flexible work arrangements, revitalizing community spaces where chance encounters occur, or leveraging technology to enhance urban mobility. By understanding and addressing the underlying causes of decreased urban diversity, we can promote a more resilient and dynamic urban environment. Utilizing data-driven human-centric approaches, we can create a more cohesive and vibrant urban setting that effectively balances individual needs and social solidarity. In the process, this can also help build trust in institutions by empowering individuals to once again effectively navigate and contribute to their urban environments. Ultimately, the restoration of urban diversity will have a significant impact on community resilience, outlasting the pandemic and its related social consequences. Our research findings serve as a call to action for further study, discussion, and community engagement on the long-term effects of the pandemic on urban settings and their diversity. Furthermore, this can lead to the development of strategies to effectively mitigate these consequences. The associated data and code used in this research are available for further review. Additional files containing supplementary material are included at the end of this report. The related work is listed in Section 9. To the best of our knowledge, this research is the first study demonstrating a substantial decline in urban diversity resulting from COVID-19-related mobility restrictions, which significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, substantially decreasing diversity by 15% to 30%. Since the optimization problem is complex and difficult to solve, a tight approximation is first used to simplify the outage probability, then energy efficiency is re-expressed in a different form and the optimization problem is re-cast into a solvable form as a mixed-integer non-linear problem for which a modified version of the \acp{ga} is an efficient and simple solution-finding method. A comparison with the direct network coding approach confirms the superiority of the maximum diversity network coding technique in terms of energy efficiency. Additionally, the research evaluates the performance of a modified genetic algorithm method that aims to reduce power consumption, as well as its ability to meet specified requirements. This study provides a lower and an upper bound for energy efficiency, as well as conditions that ensure the feasibility of the optimization problem. A numerical evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method, showing that it achieves a 60\% reduction in power consumption compared to the direct network coding technique, and the genetic algorithm variant achieves a 35\% reduction, indicating that the modified diversity network coding technique is a better option than the direct and genetic algebra variants in terms of energy efficiency. , femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering swift changes within the material's electronic system that unfold over the duration of the pulse. The amount of X-rays absorbed by the material becomes contingent upon the energy flux, giving rise to a unique form of X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy. Researchers can study valence excitation on the few-femtosecond timescale with this type of XANES spectroscopy, allowing for in-depth examination of electronic dynamics.

By analyzing copper nitride, researchers have found its response to high energy excitation. Upon being exposed to high-intensity X-ray pulses, copper nitride undergoes a significant increase in nitogen 1s photoions, with about one percent of the material being ionized per gigawatt of X-ray pulse power. The nitogen 1s absorption spectrum around a few tens of eV above the binding energy becomes distorted due to excessive ionization, developing a characteristic "white line". By applying a simple rate-based model, researchers have found that this intense redshift in the XANES spectrum results from a high propensity of nitogen 2p states to absorb excess electrons. Furthermore, researchers have found that electronic relaxation occurs within the duration of the X-ray pulse. The investigation reveals that when solid materials are subjected to intense, short-pulsed radiation, their absorption mechanisms become significantly influenced by quantitative photoionization and subtle interactions between mixed electronic states. Consequently, researchers have realized the feasibility of performing fast, atom-specific chemistry on the few-femtosecond timescale. The ability to control electronic dynamics may also open up a range of new possibilities. The research further suggests evaluating the charge state of an atom in a molecule through XANES spectroscopy, offering a new method for determining electronic configurations. The research has also explored the possibility of creating novel, short-lived metallic layers with widths on the angstrom scale by subjecting the copper layer to radiation. The investigation has found that this technique can greatly increase the reactivity of copper, creating a highly reactive copper atom with a significantly distorted electronic system that has a strong affinity for attracting other atoms to form new chemical bonds upon being released from the copper layer. In conclusion, researchers have successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of employing intense, short-pulsed X-ray pulses to explore and manipulate the intricacies of chemical bonding, photoionization, and electronic dynamics within matter. Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits significant advantages in terms of classification performance and computational efficiency over conventional methods. However, current AMC research often disregards the protection of sensitive information during the training process of Deep Neural Networks. Since AMC systems collect channel data as input, they can inadvertently obtain classified sensitive information, such as the operations being performed or the data being transmitted. We propose a method to process this data in a secure manner, using Multi-Level Homomorphic Encryption. This encryption method is applied to the AMC dataset from Germany's 5G-Arc project. We evaluate the effects of noise on the dataset and investigate the computational expense of the AMC model after the application of both LHE and Fully Homomorphic Encryption. Our study seeks to determine the feasibility of AMC under both encryption schemes. We found that the LHE approach reduces the dataset's size by 75% and incurs a considerable runtime cost of 47 seconds per epoch, although this still enables reliable modulation classification. We found FHE to be unsuitable for AMC due to excessive computational expense, with an estimated 36 hours per epoch and a substantial loss of data size of 99%. Notably, the output noise from the encrypted inputs matches the accuracy of the non-encrypted outputs, showcasing the efficacy of our proposed method. This method can potentially be applied to other communication systems as well as other Deep Neural Networks that process large datasets in an insecure setting, providing protection for sensitive information. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into epistemic and aleatoric components, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental results show that the general uncertainty model outperforms other steganographic techniques in the realm of both secure data embedding and accurate theft detection. Notably, the model's ability to estimate accurate uncertainty metrics translates to the substantial improvement of statistical steganalyser. Such a technique offers a valuable assessment of steganographic lawfulness without the need for any specific set of steganographic images. Moreover, we introduce a novel statistical test that utilizes the predictive distribution for forming decision-making, which differentiates itself from previous approaches that only utilized mean and variance values. Overall, the model's success in integrating the epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties marks a noteworthy step forward in the development of more reliable steganography-based systems. These systems are now capable of accurately quantify their internal ambiguities and external uncertainties. Consequently, such models have the potential to be applied in a diverse range of real-world steganographic scenarios. The proposed modification involves a novel combination of the prox-regular moving set and two types of perturbations: an external force acting on the solution and an internal constraint arising from a pre-stress, previously studied in the context of the static Moreau's sliding process. By integrating elements from both the subdifferential of a convex function and the gradient of a smooth function, the pre-stress constraint adds an additional layer of complexity to the problem. To address the resulting challenges, a semigroup approach is established for the first time in the literature on sweeping processes, enabling a detailed analysis of the solution using resolvents, well-posedness, a variational inequality, and a continuous dependence estimate. Furthermore, the paper provides an in-depth example illustrating the interplay between the different components of the problem. Consequently, the results established here can be considered as a rigorous mathematical justification for a previously modeled instance of surface sliding in the context of structural mechanics. Moreover, the paper shows that a particular case corresponds to a model describing 'plastic scrubbing' which has been applied in the context of de-icing techniques, as reported in recent studies. To the best of our knowledge, the results presented in this paper are a first attempt to address this specific combination of moving set, perturbations, and pre-stress within the framework of differential systems, establishing a novel contribution of this research. Ultimately, the paper showcases the versatility of the sweeping process as a fundamental tool for modeling various phenomena in the physical sciences, as well as their first-order PDE limits. Specifically, the paradigm's compatibility with IBM's Alvele algorithm, which is optimized for CPU parallelism, is demonstrated using a t-SVD calculation example on a 256 CPU node IBM Spectrum LSF cluster. challenge exists in assessing the effects of interventions on multiple units and outcomes using time-series data from observational settings. To address this issue, we've devised a novel method combining established approaches based on the factor analysis model with a Bayesian inference framework. Our proposed method uniquely allows for simultaneous handling of mixed outcome types (continuous, binomial, count), enhances causal effect estimates by modeling multiple related outcomes jointly, and provides comprehensive uncertainty quantification for desired causal estimates. Utilizing this approach, we've examined the local tracing partnerships' impact on the COVID-19 Test and Trace program's success in England and discovered that, overall, these partnerships yielded a modest, positive outcome; however, the effects exhibited considerable heterogeneity across different units and time points. Additionally, we found that the increase in COVID-19 cases among close contacts was balanced by a decrease in community infections, indicating a positive effect of the contact tracing interventions. On a methodological note, we observed that a large portion of casual effect estimates were located outside the 95% credible interval, issuing a warning about the over-interpretation of such fine-grained causal effect estimates. Our findings will be presented at an operational research conference in 2021.

This study investigates the issue of inferring constraints from observational data of an agent's compliant behavior. Experimental validation is performed to verify that the proposed method successfully identifies the most relevant constraints an agent is expected to follow. Furthermore, these constraints can be generalized and applied to novel agents with different structures and reward schemes. In contrast to existing methods that are primarily designed for tabular settings, specific types of constraints, or assume environment dynamics, the presented framework can autonomously learn any type of Markovian constraint within complex high-dimensional environments without the need for model-based representations. Overall, this research contributes to the field of safe RL by explicitly modeling constraint representations that can be learned in model-free settings. An implementation of the framework is available on GitHub, and results of the empirical analysis can be viewed on the project's webpage. This work is the first to address the online learning of general constraint representations for MDPs in both tabular and neural network settings, showcasing online sample efficiency and dynamic environment adaptability. In general distribution-shift scenarios, the method is capable of continuously updating its constraint representation, and subsequent policy improvements can be applied on any compatible agent, even when the representation is not perfectly accurate. This research lays the groundwork for future work to be conducted on safe RL. An additional area of the study, specifically the online projection of the learned weight matrix $\hat{W}$ onto the feasible set $\mathcal{W}_{\text{exp}}$, is still partially unsolved and may offer opportunities for further investigation. The method can be viewed as an extension of contrastive learning, and exploring the potential of combining the idea of constraint learning with other contrastive learning techniques could yield more general advancements. An investigation into the most suitable optimization method for efficiently identifying the factorization of the constraint matrix $A$ would also be beneficial to further improve the method's efficiency. An examination of the studied constraint types is relatively limited. An exploration into the application of the method to various other domains, such as spatial constraints in robotics or constraints derived from video data, may reveal more diverse potential uses, and it is possible that the method could learn other forms of constraints that have not yet been identified. Lastly, the method relies on an implicit model of the environment, and it is still unclear whether the method can learn to correct for explicit model inaccuracies, which may offer another avenue for further investigation. By considering PINNs that are trained with an underlying ordinary differential equation, we derive a strict upper limit on their prediction error, applicable even for data not included in the training phase and without prior knowledge of the true solution. Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of individual concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of all concept relationships and large, hierarchical structures. OntoPlot's novel hybrid visualisation introduces icicle plots, interactive elements, and space-efficient visual compression to effectively navigate and clarify the complex ontologies, including numerous task-defined associations. how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with the computational demands of the problem. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach - using quantum annealing - for resolving the active inference problem. This approach leverages advanced quantum hardware and associated algorithms to find an optimal solution by simulating brain function. Several key findings emerge. Firstly, implementing active inference using quantum hardware yields better accuracy than classical models. Secondly, incorporating a time delay - a necessity in quantum processing - surprisingly mirrors a time delay observed in real human decision-making. Thirdly, researchers discover that time delay for efficient solution finding scales with problem size at an exponential rate, contrasting with linear findings in classical computing. This research marks the first successful implementation of active inference on real-world quantum hardware, offering promising prospects for integrating quantum and deep learning techniques. Nevertheless, challenges remain in designing and scaling larger-scale cognitive architectures that align with the theory. This work paves the way for future research to explore this possibility. Another potential application of this approach involves human decision-making, particularly in situations involving a time delay. While time delay for efficient solution finding might seem counterintuitive at first, it aligns with the premise that delays are, in fact, necessary for complex cognitive processes. Researchers investigate time delay in relation to randomisation of the Markov decision process and find that introducing randomness yields better solution findings when there is a time delay. This finding highlights the significance of incorporating various sources of noise in models of human decision-making, particularly in tasks with multiple steps. Lastly, researchers show that time delay for efficient solution finding within the active inference framework doesn't deter the incorporation of priors - an essential component for dealing with uncertainty. However, incorporating priors results in optimal solution findings only when there is no time delay. This finding underscores the critical role of the assumption regarding the structure of the prior, and confirms that incorporating priors over state variables provides the best fit to empirical evidence. Researchers demonstrate that time delay for efficient solution finding with prior state assumes exponential growth, and propose that this time delay might be minimised through a more efficient structure of the prior, or by incorporating a form of regularization. These findings offer valuable insights for future research in both quantum and classical computing as well as human decision-making. Furthermore, the use of quantum hardware for complex cognitive architectures marks a significant step towards

systems, a novel NMT architecture called Seq2DRNN has been designed, which leverages a tree-structured DRNN (Doubly-Recurrent Neural Networks) model originally proposed in 2017 by Alvarez-Melis and Jaakola. The proposed Seq2DRNN architecture synergizes a sequential model for producing sequence-level predictions and a tree-structured model for capturing contextual syntactic information at sentence level. Crucially, this architecture enables sequential models to access syntactic trees through a tree-structured memory facility. By utilizing syntactic trees, it allows neural attention to focus on nodes that generate or affect the final translations, thereby enhancing NMT performance. Multiple experiments are conducted to assess the degrees of syntactic awareness possessed by Seq2DRNN. Notably, when boosters are integrated to increase syntactic awareness, the results indicate that Seq2DRNN can achieve significant improvements in metrics such as BLEU scores, demonstrating an 11% increase in BLEU scores on the wiki10 dataset and a 6% increase on the IATE dataset when boosted models are applied. Moreover, rather than solely relying on syntactic trees, by incorporating syntactic nodes into the translator design, Seq2DRNN shows improved robustness against syntactic tree corruption, exhibiting up to 2% relative drop in BLEU scores on the wiki10 dataset with 50% tree corruption. We have made the implementation of this architecture publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhongyu01/Seq2DRNN. Similar to prior syntax-aware NMT approaches, Seq2DRNN relies on manually annotated syntactic trees as input to the translator, which can be a limitation due to the complex nature of tree structures and the resources required to create them. As an alternative, this study explores the utilization of syntactic awareness boosters to increase syntactic awareness and facilitate the generation of syntactic trees. We evaluate the boosters on the wiki10 and IATE datasets, achieving an 11% and 6% increase in BLEU scores, respectively. To combat this, Knowledge Distillation is an often-used method to create high-performance yet lightweight models. This study initially assesses its application in compressing MT models, particularly for languages with scarce training data, examining eight languages in the process. Notably, it's discovered that distillation-based model compression often falls short in these languages, prompting an exploration of other compression approaches and a multiple-encoder MT architecture that can be effectively sized down while maintaining strong performance and stability. Squeeze-and-Fy, an efficient MT architecture compression method that achieves comparable results to distillation, is another finding of this study. It's observed that eliminating knowledge transfer and preprocessing layers suffices to obtain optimal results, often leading to a substantial weight reduction. Similarly, binary knowledge graph and pruning approaches were found to be successful in reducing MT model size in languages with moderate data availability, such as Chaha and Dunganka. However, it's possible that future research could improve these approaches to support languages with the least available data. Finally, it's observed that downsizing MT models enhances its robustness to out-of-vocabulary (OVW) tokens by reducing the likelihood that critical tokens are missed during inference. This was demonstrated in Xaasuun-English, where it's observed that a compressed model improves OVW capture by 7% over its uncompressed variant. The increasing use of high-bandwidth applications such as online gaming, virtual reality, and high-definition video streaming require networks with enhanced throughput levels and reduced latency. One effective strategy for achieving these goals is to deploy multiple access points within a given area, but this also raises the challenge of identifying the most suitable access point for each device. 

This study explores the potential performance enhancements that can be achieved in home WiFi networks through the use of multiple access points, set up to offer high-throughput services efficiently. The research identifies the maximum number of devices that can be effectively supported in different environmental conditions and showcases the benefits of using multiple access points, in terms of improved throughput and reduced latency in real-world applications. The investigation also reveals that deploying multiple access points leads to significant increases in the maximum bandwidth that can be delivered to each device. The findings emphasize that using multiple access points is a necessary step for enabling very high-bandwidth services over next-generation home WiFi networks. 

One of the key contributions of this research is the development of a theoretical model that identifies the most suitable access point for each device by analyzing the strength of the wireless signals received from different access points. The model can be applied in various scenarios, including different shapes and sizes of indoor environments and under distinct signal attenuation conditions. This makes it a versatile approach that can adapt to a range of different wireless configurations. 

This study further examines how to identify the most suitable access point for each device when there are multiple possible paths to follow, by developing an iterative learning model that uses historical signal data to determine the most effective routing options and allows devices to switch to a better access point when a more efficient path becomes available. The research shows that using this learning model yields significant performance improvements, with throughputs being approximately 1.6 times greater than with a simple random routing strategy. The study also finds that using a more complex random routing model that takes into account different signal levels can achieve even higher throughputs, but does not provide a practical solution for real-world applications. 

To overcome the limitations of these approaches, this research proposes an energy-efficient method for identifying the most suitable access point for each device by minimizing the energy spent on signal measurement and access point selection. The study shows that this method allows significant power savings, with energy reductions of 50 times or more for different numbers of access points and devices.
